Topic: The Brachistochrone Problem: The Path of Fastest Descent

Target audience: Senior High School or First-year University Students (Physics/Calculus interest)

Section: section_1 — The Racing Paradox

Lecture lines:
Which path gets a marble from A to B fastest?
A straight line is the shortest distance.
But is it the fastest path?
Let's race marbles on different curves.
Surprisingly, the straight line loses the race.

Planned animations:
Display Point A and Point B with labels (#FFFFFF).
Draw three paths: Straight Line (#FF4444), Deep Curve (#44FF44), and Steepest Curve (#4444FF).
Start the race: Marbles (#FFFFFF) traverse the paths at different speeds.
Highlight the Steepest Curve (#4444FF) as it finishes first.

Section: section_2 — Prerequisite Knowledge: The Speed-Height Relationship

Lecture lines:
Velocity depends on the vertical distance dropped.
Energy conservation dictates speed increases with depth.
A steeper initial drop grants higher velocity early.

Planned animations:
Write the formula v = sqrt(2gy) in bright yellow (#FFFF00).
Animate a block falling, leaving a trail of velocity vectors (#00FFFF).
Display a dynamic speedometer (#FFA500) that scales with the block's height.

Section: section_3 — Prerequisite Knowledge: Snell's Law and Light

Lecture lines:
Light always follows the path of least time.
Snell's Law describes how light bends between media.
Light curves to spend more time in faster zones.

Planned animations:
Show a ray of light (#FFFFFF) entering a medium and bending.
Label angles and the formula n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2) (#FFFF00).
Simulate light passing through thin layers with decreasing refractive indices (#888888).

Section: section_4 — The 'Aha!' Moment: Mechanical Light

Lecture lines:
Imagine the vertical space as many thin layers.
The marble speeds up as it crosses each layer.
This is exactly how light behaves in varying media.
The fastest descent follows the path of light.
This link reveals the optimal descent curve.

Planned animations:
Overlay horizontal grid lines (#333333) representing speed boundaries.
Animate a marble path (#00FF00) breaking into segments at each boundary.
Morph the segmented path into a single smooth curve (#FF00FF).

Section: section_5 — The Solution: The Cycloid

Lecture lines:
This optimal path is called a cycloid.
A cycloid is traced by a point on a rolling wheel.
It perfectly balances high speed and short distance.
Mathematics proves the cycloid is the fastest.

Planned animations:
Draw a circle (#CCCCCC) and a red dot (#FF0000) on its edge.
Roll the circle; the dot traces a cycloid path (#00FFFF).
Scale the cycloid to fit the screen and label it 'Cycloid' (#FFFF00).

Section: section_6 — The Tautochrone Property & Real-world Application

Lecture lines:
The cycloid is also a tautochrone curve.
Objects released from any height finish together.
This property is used in clocks and engineering.

Planned animations:
Create a large green cycloid ramp (#00FF00).
Place three marbles (#FF0000, #0000FF, #FFFFFF) at different heights.
Release marbles; show them meeting at the bottom simultaneously (#FFFF00 flash).
